name: Solresol, the musical language
description: Jean-François Sudre began presenting Solresol in 1817. It is built on the seven solfège syllables do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si. His book Langue musicale universelle appeared posthumously in 1866.
failedFuture: A universal language that could be sung, whistled or played on instruments. It had a brief spell of popularity in the late nineteenth century and today survives only in small groups of enthusiasts.

name: Volapük, the first planned world language
description: Johann Martin Schleyer published a sketch of Volapük in May 1879 and a full book in 1880. By 1889 there were an estimated 283 clubs, and the language claimed nearly a million adherents.
failedFuture: A global language that collapsed within a decade. Internal conflicts and schisms, together with the rise of Esperanto, drew speakers away.

name: Latino sine flexione, Peano's simplified Latin
description: Giuseppe Peano published De Latino sine flexione in 1903, a simplified form of Latin that keeps its vocabulary. At the 1907 Paris delegation Peano declared for it, but he could not take part in the final vote.
failedFuture: A Latin-based auxiliary language meant to be learned in weeks. Mathematicians were largely put off by its artificial appearance, and it was never adopted as an international language.

name: Ro, an a priori language of categories
description: Rev. Edward Powell Foster began building Ro in 1904 and issued the first booklet about it in 1906. Words are formed from a category system, so related concepts share prefixes; for example, words beginning with 'bofo-' denote colours.
failedFuture: A language whose vocabulary was meant to be logical from the ground up. The text finds no evidence that it was ever adopted; the only official act was a 1914 House resolution sent to committee.

name: Ido, the Esperanto reform
description: Ido was created in 1907 as a reform of Esperanto. Louis Couturat formed the Delegation for the Adoption of an International Auxiliary Language; the language was devised mainly by Louis de Beaufront.
failedFuture: A schism that split the planned-language movement. The article describes it as a small community today, with an estimated 500 active speakers, while newer statistics suggest 1,000 to 5,000.

name: The Futurist Manifesto
description: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the Manifesto of Futurism on 5 February 1909 in La gazzetta dell'Emilia. Le Figaro reprinted it on 20 February 1909.
failedFuture: A movement built on speed and the destruction of the old. The 1914 rift between the Milan and Florence groups weakened it, and the Great War ended its coherent existence.

name: Proletkult, the proletarian culture organisation
description: Proletkult was founded in October 1917; its first conference met in Petrograd from 16 to 19 October. In 1920 Lenin pushed through a decision to absorb it into the People's Commissariat of Education (Narkompros), with a Central Committee decree published on 1 December 1920.
failedFuture: An autonomous workers' culture movement that was absorbed into the state. The stated reason was to end the overlap of functions with Narkompros.

name: The Bauhaus, Weimar and Berlin
description: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar on 1 April 1919. Its last location was Berlin, where it closed in 1933.
failedFuture: A school that aimed to join art, craft and technology. Its leadership shut it under pressure from the Nazi regime, which had branded it a centre of communist intellectualism.

name: The League of Nations
description: The League of Nations' Covenant took effect with the Treaty of Versailles on 10 January 1920, and the Council first met on 16 January 1920.
failedFuture: An organisation meant to prevent war that did not enforce its own decisions. The United States never joined; Japan and Germany left in 1933, Italy in 1937 and Spain in 1939. The League lacked its own armed force.

description: Edgar de Wahl announced Occidental in 1922 with the first issue of Cosmoglotta in Tallinn. It was renamed Interlingue in 1949, to show neutrality towards the Soviet Union and to prepare for closer ties with Interlingua.
failedFuture: A language popular in Europe before the war. WWII disrupted it: it was banned in Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia. The major decline followed Interlingua's 1951 debut.

name: Yañalif, the Latin alphabet for Soviet Turkic languages
description: Yañalif, a Latin-based alphabet devised for Turkic languages, was adopted in Tatarstan in 1927; its final version came in 1928. It was used for Tatar and Bashkir and other Soviet languages.
failedFuture: Soviet Latinisation ended with a ban. The government prohibited Yañalif in 1939, and it remained in use until January 1940, when the switch to Cyrillic was complete. Learning two alphabets was considered problematic.

description: Latinxua Sin Wenz, a Latin-based script for Chinese, was established in 1931 through the work of Soviet sinologists and Moscow-based Chinese scholars, including Qu Qiubai. A prototype had been devised in 1929.

name: The Sun Language Theory
description: Turkish linguists of the Turkish Language Society developed the Sun Language Theory over about ten months in late 1935 and early 1936, presenting it at the Third Turkish Language Congress. It claims all languages descend from a proto-Turkic primal language.
failedFuture: A state-backed theory that Turkish was the source of all languages. It lost its prominent role shortly after Atatürk's death in November 1938, and it was not mentioned at the 1942 Turkish Language Congress.

name: The Hall of Records at Mount Rushmore
description: Excavation for a Hall of Records behind the Mount Rushmore monument began in July 1938. The chamber was to hold records of American history and aspirations, including the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, and busts of more than twenty prominent Americans.
failedFuture: A time capsule that was never finished. The federal government ordered work stopped about a year into construction, around 1939. In 1998 sixteen porcelain enamel panels were sealed in a vault beneath a granite capstone.

name: Lincos, a language for cosmic intercourse
description: Hans Freudenthal described Lincos in 1960 in Lincos: Design of a Language for Cosmic Intercourse, Part 1. It was designed to be understandable by any intelligent extraterrestrial life form, for interstellar radio transmissions.
